title: Recursive Backtracking
body:
Search by recursion: extend a partial solution one choice at a time, recurse, and when a choice
leads nowhere, undo it and try the next. It is the technique the functional model makes
natural, because "try every branch and collect what works" is a description of a list rather
than a description of a procedure.

[[Backtracking]] in the `Leetcode/` set is the imperative version and it is worth reading first
for the choose / explore / unchoose discipline and the `path.pop()` that undoes a move. This
note is about what changes when there is nothing to undo.

## The undo disappears

In a mutable language the shared `path` is the whole difficulty: you must pop exactly what you
pushed, on every exit path, or later branches inherit corrupted state. With [[Immutability]]
there is no shared path. Each recursive call receives its own value, so nothing needs restoring:

```haskell
queens :: Int -> [ [Int] ]
queens n = go n
  where
    go 0 = [[]]                                  -- one solution: the empty board
    go k = [ q : qs | qs <- go (k - 1)           -- every solution for k-1 rows
                    , q  <- [1 .. n]             -- every column for this row
                    , safe q qs ]                -- keep the ones that do not attack

    safe q qs = and [ q /= c && abs (q - c) /= d
                    | (d, c) <- zip [1 ..] qs ]
```

That is all of n-queens. There is no explicit stack, no visited set to reset, and no `unchoose`
step, because `qs` is never modified. The [[List Comprehension]] *is* the search: generators
are the choices and guards are the pruning.

## It is the list monad

The comprehension above desugars to `concatMap`, which is `>>=` for lists, so the search is a
[[Monad]] computation:

```haskell
go k = go (k - 1) >>= \qs -> [1 .. n] >>= \q -> if safe q qs then [q : qs] else []
```

`return x` is `[x]` (one solution), `[]` is failure, and `>>=` is "for every result so far, try
every continuation". This is the best link the course has to
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: it is exactly the explore-all-branches reading of
[[Nondeterminism]]. An [[NFA]] accepts if *some* path accepts; the list monad returns *every*
path that succeeds. The nondeterministic machine is the specification and the list monad is the
implementation, which is why "guess the right branch" is a legitimate way to write code here
and not just a proof device.

The same equivalence explains logic programming: Prolog's execution model is this search with
unification supplying the choices.

## Laziness does the pruning

`head (queens 8)` computes one solution and stops. Not "computes 92 and returns the first":
[[Lazy Evaluation]] means the generators past the first success are never run at all. So the
generate-everything phrasing above, which looks catastrophically wasteful, costs the same as a
hand-pruned depth-first search. That is the strongest practical demonstration of laziness in
the course.

Pruning still matters where it changes the *shape* of the tree rather than its length: `safe q
qs` is checked before recursing deeper, so whole subtrees never exist. The rule is the same one
[[Backtracking]] gives, prune before you recurse, not after.

## Core Facts to Know

- Extend a partial solution, recurse, and abandon branches that violate a constraint.
- Depth-first over the tree of choices; see [[Depth First Search]].
- With [[Immutability]] there is no undo step: each call has its own copy and nothing is shared.
- A [[List Comprehension]] with generators as choices and guards as pruning *is* the search.
- Generators desugar to `concatMap` = `>>=`, so backtracking is the **list [[Monad]]**.
- `[]` is failure and `[x]` is one success, so the monad handles the bookkeeping.
- It is the explore-all-branches reading of [[Nondeterminism]], made executable.
- [[Lazy Evaluation]] means `head` of the results stops the search at the first solution.
- Prune before recursing so that dead subtrees are never generated.
- Prolog's execution model is this plus unification.
